stories.headline: Open covenants openly arrived at
stories.title: Open covenants openly arrived at
stories.summary: More than a century ago, American President Woodrow Wilson stood before Congress and articulated a clear vision for international order. His very first principle was simple yet revolutionary, calling for “ open covenants of peace that were openly arrived at” . Wilson believed that the devastating conflicts of his era were fuelled by secret alliances and private understandings struck by powerful leaders behind closed doors. In his view, durable peace required transparency, public accountability, and the inclusion of all nations affected by global decisions. Today, that famous dictum has returned to the center of international debate following the historic trilateral summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, where United States President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and Chinese President Xi Jinping met behind closed doors on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. While the three leaders emerged with a joint declaration toward peace, foreign policy analysts, diplomats, and international observers remain deeply divided over whether the gathering represents a pragmatic step toward global stability or a troubling retreat from inclusive multilateralism. Proponents of realist diplomacy and supporters of the Shenzhen meeting argue first and foremost that direct communication among Washington, Moscow, and Beijing is both practical and urgently necessary. As Trump emphasised during the talks, refusing to engage with rival powers solves no problems, and when dialogue between the world’s largest military powers freezes, the risk of miscalculation and accidental conflict rises sharply. By sitting together at one table, the three leaders demonstrated that high level diplomacy remains active even during periods of deep geopolitical rivalry. Realists also point to specific areas of convergence in the joint declaration. The three nations committed to increasing the production and supply of refined oil products to support steady global energy flows, a move welcomed by economists concerned about supply chain disruptions in developing nations. Furthermore, following the expiration of the New START nuclear treaty in February, the world has been left without legally binding limits on strategic nuclear weapons. Although the leaders did not sign a new treaty in Shenzhen, supporters emphasize that their pledge to continue discussions on reducing nuclear risks serves as an important stabilising mechanism, while their joint call to reform the United Nations acknowledges that international institutions must evolve to reflect contemporary global realities. Conversely, sceptics, legal experts, and representatives of smaller nations contend that the Shenzhen summit undermines the core principles of rules based multilateralism. Several foreign policy commentators have compared the gathering to the Yalta Conference of 1945, where dominant powers discussed spheres of influence without the consent of smaller countries. Sceptics point to the omission of major ongoing conflicts from the final joint statement as a primary flaw, noting that although the war in Ukraine has entered its fifth year, the declaration made no mention of Ukraine or the conflict in Iran at all. European diplomats and analysts have argued that discussing broader security arrangements without European allies or Ukrainian representatives in the room runs counter to Wilsonian ideals of fair representation and transparency. Beyond the exclusion of key stakeholders, legal experts and human rights advocates have raised strong objections to the declaration’s stance on international justice. In their joint statement, Washington, Moscow, and Beijing warned the International Criminal Court against overreach and asserted broad immunity for state officials. Sceptics argue that when the world’s three strongest military powers unite to curb international legal bodies, it weakens the institutional protections that smaller states rely upon against aggression by stronger neighbours. Finally, many observers remain deeply doubtful about the practical substance behind the summit’s broader institutional pledges. Arms control specialists note that reaffirming general slogans against nuclear war falls far short of concrete verification measures or binding limits. Similarly, diplomats from emerging powers such as India and members of the African Union have long argued that genuine United Nations reform requires expanding permanent representation on the Security Council with veto power rather than merely restructuring agencies to suit great power convenience. Ultimately, while realists view direct engagement among major powers as a necessary safety valve, the Shenzhen trilateral reveals the grave danger of replacing inclusive diplomacy with an exclusive club of giants. Woodrow Wilson rightly warned that agreements crafted in secret by dominant powers rarely produce durable legitimacy. By sidelining affected nations, weakening international courts, and offering symbolism in place of binding commitments, the Shenzhen summit risks eroding the very multilateral order upon which lasting global peace depends. The write is a Kashmir based academic and teaches Political Science in the Higher Education Department of J&K.

stories.headline: Reservations: Karnataka to Kashmir
stories.title: Reservations: Karnataka to Kashmir
stories.summary: Striking down a state law that had increased reservations in educational institutions and appointments or posts in the services under the State beyond the permissible constitutional limit, the Karnataka High Court has reiterated that breaching the 50 per cent quota cap undermines the right to equality and equal opportunity guaranteed under Articles 14, 15 and 16 of the Constitution of India. The Jammu and Kashmir High Court has also admitted and sought the government’s response to multiple petitions challenging the reservation policy in the region. It may be noted that, in J&K, reservations have risen to 70 per cent and candidates in the open-merit category constitute nearly 69 per cent of the population are competing for just 30 per cent of the jobs. The worry is that behind every statistic is a depressed but highly educated student who may also not be privileged. Martin Luther King warned that “injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere”. It is in this context that the Karnataka case assumes significance. Karnataka High Court Verdict A Bench of the Karnataka High Court, headed by Chief Justice Vibhu Bakhru, declared Sections 3 and 4 of the Karnataka Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Reservation of Seats in Educational Institutions and of Appointments or Posts in the Services under the State) Act, 2022, unconstitutional. The 2022 ordinance was replaced by legislation enhancing state-level reservations for Scheduled Castes from 15 to 17 per cent and for Scheduled Tribes from 3 to 7 per cent. This pushed the State’s aggregate affirmative-action quota from 50 to 56 per cent, while the unreserved pool available to open-merit candidates was reduced from 50 to 44 per cent. The petitioners challenged the increase in reservations to 56 per cent as violative of Articles 14, 15 and 16 of the Constitution. They also submitted that decisions of Supreme Court Constitution Benches—including M.R. Balaji v. State of Mysore, Indra Sawhney v. Union of India, M. Nagaraj v. Union of India and Dr. Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil v. Chief Minister—had established a 50 per cent ceiling that was binding and not flexible. The judgment observed that breaching the 50 per cent “ceiling” could lead to reverse discrimination. The Court further made it clear that Article 16(1) mandates adequate representation, not proportionate representation based on census figures. Many observers believe that the State failed to demonstrate the existence of extraordinary circumstances that could justify exceeding the 50 per cent ceiling. Several surveys have highlighted the rise in unemployment and the loss of jobs in Karnataka, a State that possesses considerable potential to attract investment. Interestingly, amid all this, the Karnataka Government issued an order reviving campus elections after a gap of 37 years, allowing young people to deliberate on issues concerning their future. In Jammu and Kashmir, the reservation issue has become explosive and combustible. In the opinion of many people, it has been weaponised to empower some categories while disempowering others. Open-Merit Margins After the fall of the BJP–PDP coalition government in J&K in 2018 and the imposition of central rule, the reservation pendulum shifted rapidly. The BJP-led government extended a maximum of 10 per cent reservation to Economically Weaker Sections, in line with the policy at the national level. After the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes approved the inclusion of the Pahari community in the Scheduled Tribes list, the Lok Sabha passed the J&K Reservation (Amendment) Bill in December 2023. The legislation provided the Paharis with reservation in jobs, education and the J&K Legislature under the Scheduled Tribes category. The subsequent notification stipulated that the Paharis would receive 10 per cent reservation, taking the Scheduled Tribes quota to 20 per cent. The Administrative Council, headed by the Lieutenant Governor, also sanctioned the inclusion of 15 more communities in the OBC category, enhanced the reservation for OBCs to 8 per cent, and reduced the reservation for Residents of Backward Areas (RBA) from 20 to 10 per cent. These changes increased the overall reservation to 70 per cent. The actual implementation of the new reservation framework has dealt thousand cuts to students from the Kashmir region, particularly when the issuance of various types of certificates in Jammu and Kashmir is examined separately. Why this is so, is a question that needs to be answered rationally? Politics vs. Policy Prominent BJP leader and then in-charge of Kashmir affairs, Mr. Ram Madhav, stated unambiguously in 2024 that the main issue in J&K was Jammu’s prominence and political unity. He referred to Ghulam Nabi Azad’s brief tenure as Chief Minister, during which he represented Jammu. (The Indian Express, September 28, 2024.) The two issues that generated considerable controversy after the reorganisation of Jammu and Kashmir in 2019 were delimitation and reservation. Both, according to critics, have favoured Jammu’s prominence. The delimitation exercise appeared predetermined, as it had already recommended the creation of seven additional seats. Jammu received six additional seats, compared with only one additional seat for Kashmir. The reservation issue, too, appears to favour Jammu when regional politics and the distribution of different categories are examined. First, approximately 85 per cent of the entire Scheduled Caste population resides in the districts of Udhampur, Jammu, Samba and Kathua, as well as in the Reasi subdivision, with the remainder dispersed across the other parts of the Jammu division. Furthermore, 68 per cent of Scheduled Tribes, 72 per cent of Pahari-speaking people and 93 per cent of residents living near the Line of Control are domiciled in the Jammu division. Residents of areas adjoining the International Border were brought within the reservation system along with those living near the Line of Control. As of today, approximately 268 villages are located near the LoC, while 551 villages adjoin the International Border. Only the Residents of Backward Areas and Other Social Castes are distributed relatively evenly across Jammu and Kashmir. Second, the reservation system has now become a source of regional exclusion and discrimination. One legislator said that the “whole system is rigged against Kashmiris.” According to information furnished to the Union Territory legislature during its recent session, nearly 11.81 lakh reservation certificates had been issued across seven categories in J&K. Of these, 86 per cent were issued in Jammu and only 14 per cent in Kashmir—by no means a marginal difference. Meanwhile, the Jammu and Kashmir Public Service Commission and the Services Selection Board have collected Rs 113.9 crore from job seekers over the past three years, as disclosed in the Assembly. This may be good news for a revenue-starved government which simultaneously has questioned the policy. Reactions of Political Leaders The president of the Apni Party, Mr. Altaf Bukhari, recently described the existing reservation policy as “unjust, detrimental and unfair to the people of Kashmir, who have already suffered immensely over the decades.” He further stated that “two lakh Kashmiris are buried in graveyards, thousands are languishing in jails, and now people are being deprived even of employment opportunities.” He argued that an unjust reservation policy violated human rights. Mr. Sajjad Lone of the People’s Conference described the policy as “recruitment apartheid,” while Iltija Mufti of the PDP called it “reservation apartheid against open-merit students in Kashmir.” Opinion leaders and members of civil society believe that the policy is discriminatory and was prepared in haste. The youth in Kashmir are struggling with basic milestones, such as getting married and having children. This generation cannot imagine achieving these things within the next decade. This creates anxiety about what it means to become an adult. Young people are hoping for change but feel that the system as a whole is suffering from a crisis of legitimacy. As I write this column, serious questions are being raised about the examination for Finance Accounts Assistants conducted by the Services Selection Board. In light of the foregoing discussion, policymakers—and state managers —need to examine the merits of certain proposals put forward by eminent individuals from time to time. First, the Anand Committee, chaired by the late Justice A.S. Anand, was constituted under Government Order No. 540-GR of 1976, dated August 24, 1976. The Committee marked a shift towards identifying socially and educationally backward classes through an area-specific approach based on social, educational and economic indicators. In Jammu and Kashmir- a miniature India—the region should be treated as the basic unit of identification. Second is the “Drabu formulation,” proposed by economist Haseeb Drabu. He suggested that the 8 per cent reservation for Scheduled Castes should be confined to the Jammu division, while the Kashmir region should have no reservation for Scheduled Castes. He proposed that the 20 per cent reservation for Scheduled Tribes be rationalised by providing 15 per cent in Jammu and 10 per cent in Kashmir. He further suggested reducing the existing reservation for Economically Weaker Sections to 7 per cent in both regions and limiting the reservation for people living along the Line of Control and the International Border to 2 per cent, replacing the existing 4 per cent. The 8 per cent reservation for OBCs, he argued, should remain intact in both regions. Under this arrangement, the open-merit quota would increase to 50 per cent in Jammu and 63 per cent in Kashmir. Third, formulation is to examine the merits of a sub-regional model of reservation. In undivided Jammu and Kashmir, the potential of sub-regional councils for Leh and Kargil was recognised through the establishment of hill councils. During my study of these councils and my interactions with elected representatives in Leh and Kargil, I observed considerable enthusiasm about the new institutional arrangement and the resulting changes in the work culture. In Maharashtra, sub-regional arrangements for Vidarbha, Marathwada and the rest of Maharashtra are explicitly recognised under Article 371(2) of the Constitution of India. A sub-regional model of reservation could promote equity and address concerns relating to social justice. To conclude, in Jammu and Kashmir, it was only from 1968 onwards that the government-initiated recruitment system became relatively free from political interference. Unfortunately, in the new administrative arrangement, according to the 2011 Census, the open-merit category—comprising 69 per cent of the population—is competing for only 30 per cent of government jobs. The All-India Lawyers Union has rightly observed that unemployment is rooted in systemic policy failures. Prof. Gull Mohammad Wani, a Kashmir-based political scientist.
